 By Amber Middleton 
 Judi Dench, 91, Follows This Japanese Longevity Secret Without
Even Realizing It — and It Could Be the Key to Living Longer
 It's backed by science.
Getty: Samir Hussein 
 At 91, Judi Dench has had a long
and versatile career. She’s known for playing M in 
James Bond , she acted in Shakespeare in Love, and has been on
stage at the theatre countless times over the years. 
 She’s critically acclaimed for
the work she’s done too — she has an Oscar, a Tony, two Golden
Globes, six BAFTAs and seven Olivier Awards. But she’s absolutely
not done yet. 
 Her memoirist and friend,
Brendan O’Hea shares quotes in The Times , of where Judi explains that there
are lots of parts of ageing that she doesn’t enjoy. “You have to
contend with people asking, ‘When are you going to retire?’ or,
‘Isn’t it about time you put your feet up?’ No, it bloody well
isn’t,” she says. 
 Instead, she wants to keep
working for a while yet. “I want to be like Newton Blick, who died
in his dressing room after a performance,” she says of the
Hollywood actor made famous in the 1950s. “I want to be one of
those women who throw themselves out of planes when they’re
100.” 
 And while it might not sound
like the best way to 
live into old age , there is some science to suggest she’s
following a longevity hack. 
Judi Dench with James Bond costar, Daniel Craig and director Marc
Forster, Getty: Rosie Greenway 
 The Purpose-Led Longevity Hack 
 There is a concept originating
in Japan known as ‘ikigai.’ This refers to your sense of purpose,
or what gets you out of bed in the morning. The Japanese island of
Okinawa is thought to be a ‘blue zone,’ meaning they have a
particularly high number of centenarians (people living to 100).
And locals put this concept of having an ‘ikigai’ as one of the
reasons they live so long. 
 After retiring, many locals will
volunteer in their local area, look after grandchildren — or even
starting a new hobby like gardening. And r esearch has confirmed that having a purpose
like this can add years to your lifespan. 
 A 2008
study across over 43,000
Japanese adults looked into whether having this sense of purpose
could actually extend your life in old age. The results found that
over a seven year period, participants who didn’t have a
sense of purpose were significantly more likely to die of heart
problems and other external causes. 
 And another
study across US adults
gave the same result — older adults were much more likely to live
longer with some kind of purpose. 
 That’s not to say, you should
work yourself into the grave, rather find something that gets you
out of bed each morning — and it could help you 
live a long and happy life , whether it’s selling jams at the
local farmer market or throwing yourself out of planes, like Judi
suggests.
